articles.title: Kmemo 2.0 is out, and the two gaps I admitted to in the first post are closed
articles.excerpt: This is a follow-up to Kmemo: a semantic cache for LLM calls that refuses to serve you the wrong answer. If you have not read it, the one-line version is that Convert 100 USD to EUR and Convert 250 US…
articles.body: This is a follow-up to Kmemo: a semantic cache for LLM calls that refuses to serve you the wrong answer . If you have not read it, the one-line version is that Convert 100 USD to EUR and Convert 250 USD to EUR sit at 0.99 cosine similarity, no threshold separates them, and Kmemo reads the candidates as text instead of trusting the number. That post shipped 1.0 and ended with two things I could not report. 2.0.0 is out now, and both of them have an answer. One of the answers is not the one I was hoping for. Gap one: I never said what a verifier catches The figures in the first post were 67% of near misses rejected and 88% of paraphrases kept, and I labelled them guard-only. The lexical chain runs for free; the optional Verifier is a model call that sees whatever the guards let through.

articles.title: Correlated Subqueries Explained: From Confusing to Intuitive
articles.excerpt: Hey everyone! 👋 It's been a while since I posted here. Over the past few days, I've been revisiting SQL from the ground up—not just solving problems, but understanding why different SQL concepts exis…
articles.body: Hey everyone! 👋 It's been a while since I posted here. Over the past few days, I've been revisiting SQL from the ground up—not just solving problems, but understanding why different SQL concepts exist and when they should be used. One topic that confused me (and many beginners) was correlated subqueries . You may have seen queries like this: SELECT ... FROM table1 t1 WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM table2 t2 WHERE t2 . id = t1 . id ); and wondered: How is the inner query accessing columns from the outer query? When does the inner query execute? How is this different from a normal subquery? In this article, we'll answer all of these questions by solving a real SQL problem from LeetCode .

articles.excerpt: In May 2025, I published an article called Foreboding AI: The Inevitable Collapse We’re Funding Ourselves. Some people agreed with it. Others said I was being dramatic. Alarmist. Fearful. Anti-technol…
articles.body: In May 2025, I published an article called Foreboding AI: The Inevitable Collapse We’re Funding Ourselves . Some people agreed with it. Others said I was being dramatic. Alarmist. Fearful. Anti-technology. Perhaps some of the language was dramatic. The subject was dramatic. But the central warning was never that every AI system was evil, conscious, or secretly plotting humanity’s destruction. The warning was much simpler: We were developing increasingly powerful systems faster than society could understand, secure, regulate, or adapt to them. A year later, I returned to the subject in Foreboding AI, One Year Later: What Are We Really Building? By then, AI was no longer just answering questions. It was browsing websites. Reading files. Running commands. Editing codebases. Calling APIs.

articles.body: We just got an amazing new view of SpaceX's Starship vehicle, thanks to one of the company's next-gen Starlink satellites. Starship , the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, launched on its 13th test flight from South Texas last Friday (July 24). The suborbital jaunt was similar in many respects to past Starship test missions, with one big exception: This time, the vehicle deployed a batch of functional, next-gen Starlink internet satellites into space. Six of those "Starlink V3" spacecraft carried cameras, so that SpaceX could get good views of the heat shield on Starship's upper stage, which is known as Starship, or simply Ship. The satellites did that job and more, capturing amazing views of Ship as it cruised away from them high above Earth .

articles.title: How do supermassive black holes grow? AI finds 7 spacetime-warping 'quasars' that could help solve the mystery
articles.excerpt: Astronomers found seven rare quasar gravitational lens candidates using AI, providing a powerful new tool for studying black hole and galaxy evolution.
articles.body: Some of the brightest objects in the universe may also hold the key to understanding how galaxies evolve — especially when gravity transforms them into giant cosmic magnifying glasses. Using artificial intelligence to search through data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), astronomers have identified seven promising candidates for quasars acting as gravitational lenses — natural cosmic magnifying glasses created when a massive object's gravity bends and magnifies light from a more distant object. These unusual systems could help researchers better understand how actively growing supermassive black holes evolve, according to a statement from Ohio State University.

articles.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day - Our Biggest Burning Questions About the New Marvel Movie
articles.excerpt: Would a real New Yorker eat Little Caesars? We have so many burning questions from Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
articles.body: Spoilers follow for Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Is your Spider-Sense tingling? If so, it may be less of a Peter Tingle, and more of a burning sensation, as Spider-Man: Brand New Day is on fire with a lot of dangling plot points that need addressing. Sure, the movie finishes up this leg of Peter Parker’s (Tom Holland) emotional journey in a satisfying manner, and concludes his battle with the not-so-villainous Jean Elaine Grey (Sadie Sink). But there are still bad guys out there, good guys in new situations, and end credits scenes that are, let’s be honest, potentially extremely confusing. With that in mind, let’s lay out some of the biggest burning questions we have after Spider-Man: Brand New Day, as well as some of the smallest, and see how well we can do in also answering them. Thwip!

articles.title: Claude published malicious code to the Internet and attacked 3 real companies
articles.excerpt: Had the hacks used conventional methods, someone would likely go to prison.
articles.body: Anthropic said its Claude-based security models gained unauthorized access to the sensitive production environments of three outside organizations during internal testing designed to measure the models’ offensive cyber capabilities. The events, which Anthropic revealed Thursday , are the second revelation in 10 days that AI models from the world’s wealthiest providers have trespassed into protected networks, an offense that, in more traditional hacking scenarios, could land the human behind the keyboard in prison for years. Earlier this month, OpenAI said its security models exploited a zero-day vulnerability for use in breaking into the network of Hugging Face, a platform for open source machine-learning models and AI datasets.
